Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association (MMA) Neither For Nor Against
LD 1973, Resolve, to Establish the Commission to Study Oversight and Funding Structures for Recovery Residences and Resident Protections
May 19, 2025
______________________________________________________________
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, my name is Amanda Campbell, and I am submitting testimony neither for not against LD 1973 on behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's 70-member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC).
The resolve proposed in LD 1973 establishes a commission to study the policies and standards of operation for recovery residences. Municipal officials agree that with recent increases in recovery residence housing and the role local government plays in the process, a review of these policies is appropriate. This bill looks to address residences with 25 or more beds, which is important for the one municipality that is host to a residence of that scale, but it is worth noting that communities that host multiple smaller residences are facing increased financial burdens as well, funded entirely by the property taxpayers. It is possible that proposed legislation that this committee has already heard, which does not limit a stakeholder group's membership to a municipal official from a community that hosts larger facility, may achieve what the sponsor of LD 1973 is looking to achieve.
Regardless of the vehicle used to accomplish the proposed commission, or stakeholder group, municipal leaders request representation from communities hosting all sizes of recovery residences. Additionally, the proposed timeline for a report back, while ambitious, may not provide the time that this topic requires for a full vetting of the policies, administration, funding and oversight of recovery residences in Maine.
Thank you for your consideration of the municipal perspective on this important topic. Please feel free to contact any member of the LPC or the MMA Advocacy team with any questions relating to municipal operations.

Good afternoon Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and Honorable Members of the Committee on HHS,
My name is Courtney Gary-Allen, and I am the Executive Director of the Maine Recovery
R
Action Project (ME-RAP), a grassroots network of Mainers working to advance
community-driven solutions to substance use. I'm here today to testify in support of LD 1973 on
behalf of our statewide organizing team.
ME-RAP's work is grounded in the voices of people most directly impacted by Maine's addiction crisis. Last summer, we hosted 33 listening sessions across all 16 counties and heard
from over 670 Mainers. Recovery housing came up in nearly every conversation. In relation to
recovery housing, what we heard was not a single, unified viewpoint, but a wide range of lived experiences, ideas, and concerns about how recovery housing should evolve to better meet the
needs of our communities. While at times, these views were deeply conflicting--- all reflected a
shared desire to help people find safety, stability, and long-tenn recovery.
Many participants raised concems about the lack of oversight and funding in recovery housing, especially regarding the role of house managers. Many felt that these managers need more
training, support, and compensation---relying solely on free rent is not sustainable or safe.
Communities also spoke about the negative impact of local "Not In My Backyard" (NIMBY) policies, which often try to block or restrict the development of recovery homes. We heard strong
calls for more transitional recovery housing, particularly for people who are unhoused and in
long-term recovery. At the same time, participants emphasized that one size doesn't fit all: recovery looks different for everyone, and housing options need to reflect that.
One of the most polarizing issues was the role of medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) in
recovery residences. Some residents reported being denied housing because of their medications,
while others---especially those pursuing abstinence-based recovery--shared fears about being
forced to accept MOUD in ways that compromised the safety or integrity of their program. On
both sides, we heard a shared frustration: people are afraid. Abstinence-based homes fear
lawsuits or investigations for being honest about their approach, while people on medication fear being turned away.

required mandatory certification of recovery residences in Maine.
However, when we brought this proposal to our organizing team for discussion and a vote--as we do with all policy decisions---serious concems were raised:

0 Why are some recovery residence operators choosing not to pursue certification?
0 If certification fees are a barrier, will financial support be available to help recovery
residences comply?

Americans with Disabilities Act?
0 MARR's current policies prohibit the use of medical cannabis in certified recovery
residences. Would mandatory certification prevent individuals prescribed medical
cannabis from living in a recovery residence?
0 Could shutting down well-run, non-certified homes increase the risk of overdose or
homelessness for residents?

These are important questions that deserve thoughtful discussion----not rushed legislation.

Testimony ofRep. Dave Rollins introducing
LD 1973, Resolve, to Establish the Commission to Study Oversight
and Funding Structures for Recovery Residences and Resident

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
Good afternoon, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Health and
Human Services Committee, my name is Dave Rollins and I have the honor of representing
House District 59, which is half of Augusta. Today, I am here to present LD 1973, Resolve, to
Establish the Commission to Study Oversight and Funding Structures for Recovery Residences and Resident Protections.
This bill did not start out as a study commission. Originally, I intended to introduce legislation
that would have mandated certification of recovery residences in Maine by the Maine
Association of Recovery Residences, or MARR. But, after receiving significant and thoughtful
feedback from individuals across the recovery community, it became clear that this issue is more complex and more contested than any single bill could resolve in a few short weeks.
There is a real split in the recovery community around whether mandatory certification of
recovery residences is the right path forward. Some view certification as a critical tool for
ensuring safety and accountability. Others question whether certification alone is enough -- or
whether a licensure model would provide stronger and more enforceable protections. Others
would prefer we strengthen the voluntary certification that we have now. Still others point out
that MARR's existing policies ---- including its prohibition on the use of medical cannabis in certified homes -- exclude recovery residences that serve people using prescribed medicine that
is legal in Maine and, for many, lifesaving.
In this session, we've heard compelling testimony and legislative proposals from Representatives
Hasenfus, Warren and others about the growing need to better understand the impact of recovery
residences on local communities. In Winthrop, for example, there's rising concern about how
these homes affect General Assistance budgets. Representative Hasenfus emphasized the need for more analysis on key factors--such as the size and concentration of recovery residences and their financial impact on municipal assistance programs. Rep. Warren's proposal shed light on the fact that individuals in recovery who live in these residences are not eligible for BRAP--the Bridging Rental Assistance Prograrn----leaving them in a vulnerable position.

District 59: Augusta (Part)

We've also heard directly from constituents and community members about deeply troubling
practices in some uncertified houses --- including reports of people paying rent and being kicked out days later, and even instances of drug dealing occurring inside homes labeled as "recovery residences." These aren't just administrative problems --- they are life-and-death issues that
speak to a lack of standards, oversight and consistency in a space that is supposed to be centered on healing.
At the same time, we've heard from people in recovery who were denied housing in certified
recovery residences because they were on an FDA-approved and prescribed medication for
opioid use disorder.
All of this points to the urgent need for a broader, more inclusive policy conversation about what recovery housing in Maine should look like ---- and what the appropriate mechanisms for
oversight, funding and resident protections should be. We need to step back and ask: What are we trying to achieve with recovery housing? Who is being left out? And how can we create a
system that uplifts the good actors while holding bad actors accountable?
Today, MARR has certified 100 recovery residences. While I applaud how far our state has
come in terms of expanding access to recovery housing, I do think such rapid growth calls for reflection on where we have been and where we would like to go. I actually feel that it is our ethical duty given that some of our most vulnerable Mainers reside in these homes.
That conversation simply cannot be had in the compressed timeline of this legislative session.
That is why I am proposing a summer study commission ~-- a dedicated space Where a diverse
group of stakeholders, including people with lived experience, service providers, advocates and
government officials, can come together to examine the full landscape and report back to the

The intent of this legislation is to establish the Commission to Study Oversight and Funding Structures for Recovery Residences and Resident protections. This Commission would be required to evaluate various policies and industry standards, and make policy recommendations with respect to the use of general assistance and the possible expansion or development of new state-funded subsidy programs for use at a recovery residence, alternative models of oversight structure for recovery residences, including voluntary certification, mandatory certification or licensure, and policies related to the use of prescribed medications in recovery residences. The Commission would also be required to submit a report back to the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services with their findings, recommendations, and any suggested legislation.

OBH respectfully opposes this legislation. The Department, alongside the Governor's Office of Policy and Innovation & Future (GOPIF) and the Maine Association of Recovery Residences (MARR), are already participating in multiple efforts surrounding the issues that this Commission would be seeking to address. As drafted, it is not clear how this Commission would facilitate new efforts or produce new recommendations without duplicating ongoing efforts.

Additionally, the Office of Behavioral Health contracts with MARR who provides training, policy development, and certification services utilizing standards set by the National Alliance for Recovery Residences (NARR). As the state affiliate of NARR, MARR serves as a conduit for policy and operational best practices related to Recovery Residence programming. Much of what is asked for in this bill is available from MARR currently or could be provided by MARR if requested.

The issues this legislation is intending to address could in fact be reviewed and discussed without the necessity of a formal Commission. It is also worth noting that some questions surrounding General Assistance and its use and place in recovery residences are being addressed via LD 215 put forth this session and may be duplicative or counterproductive to also be addressed through

this legislation. More broadly, the Office of Family Independence engaged in the rule making process to determine eligibility and payment standards for Recovery Residences, with rules released in 2024.
Rulemaking for Recovery Residences is on the administrative docket for this Fall, and additional policy considerations may be addressed during that process, which includes public comment and revision opportunities.
